newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: YEAR - Asia growing towards energy giant.
newsitem.headline: YEAR - Asia growing towards energy giant.

text.p: Asia took another step in 1996 towards being the world's biggest consumer of energy, but some analysts said they feared economic and political constraints were weighing it down.

Europe and the United States showed every sign of consolidating, with a frenzy of mergers between oil majors, while Asia witnessed an expansion of its refining sector, new crudes and countries opening their energy markets to outside competitors.

Analysts have not yet crunched the numbers for 1996, but they said the slow pace of liberalisation, the struggle to build an infrastructure that can keep pace with demand and political changes were causing energy growth to be reined in.

"This region is not yet, and will not be for a long time yet, the largest region for energy consumption," said Trevor MacMurray, managing director of McKinsey & Co's South-East Asia energy consultancy.
"In some ways it is not important when it will happen. It is a very large market... it will happen at some point," he said.
Asia's primary energy demand was 2.48 billion tonnes of oil equivalent (toe) in 1995 (50 million barrels per day), and accounted for a quarter of the world's total consumption.
Analysts forecast growth of more than 21 percent to 3.004 billion toe by 2000, overtaking the largest consumer, North America, which is expected to reach 2.719 billion toe by the turn of the decade.

"The five percent annual growth rates in Asia since 1988 are pretty tremendous," said Al Troner, managing director of Asia Pacific Energy Consulting. "If you took out Japan it would be almost seven percent, which is pretty extraordinary."
Asia's refiners added more than 1.0 million bpd in output capacity to 17.5 million bpd. The new capacity attracted major volumes of Alaskan North Slope crude for the first time.
But refineries struggled to make decent profits because of high crude prices in 1996, which were generally $3 per barrel higher than a year earlier.
"Refining margins are much worse than they were, and we don't think they are going to get a lot better," MacMurray said. "Potentially we see a lot of projects in Asia being rethought."
China's construction of several power plants and oil refineries has been delayed in favour of making the most of existing plants.
"But it has taken a long time for that policy to work, resulting in supply constraints which means there is some unmet demand in China," MacMurray said.
Even where more aggressive expansion policies are in place, the energy infrastructure is retarded, meaning Asia will rely on imports for several years to come, Troner told Reuters.

Quoting statistics from the Honolulu-based East-West Center, Troner said Asia-Pacific's base-refining capacity, currently 21 percent of world capacity, is expected to rise over the next five years to around 24 percent, but it will be utterly inadequate to meet the region's demand.

However refinery de-bottlenecking and expansions, particularly in Thailand and South Korea, over the past year have created overcapacity and product imbalances in certain parts of the region, analysts said.

"There is a need for energy capacity and infrastructure, but it is a strange mix with oversupply, with too many gas stations in Thailand, while in other areas like China and Indonesia, there is not enough capacity," said MacMurray.
"You can't say Asia is continuing to grow very fast economically and needs more refinery capacity -- it's actually getting more mixed."
Asian governments are pushing to open up their energy sectors, but the slow pace of change would remain a restraint on growth in energy demand, analysts said.
Japan deregulated its products market in April, but a stiff 60-day stockpiling requirement left the pre-liberalisation monopoly of refiners intact.

Taiwan lifted curbs on oil imports in June, but imports are linked to existing crude production, which also leaves state-owned Chinese Petroleum Corp's position secure for a few more years because it is Taiwan's only crude producer.
Major swing buyers, China and India, lag behind most of Asia, but their huge potential markets attract major oil companies.
"Deregulation will stimulate demand and consumption," said MacMurray. "Supply tends to create demand in energy because there is latent demand there.

"But you won't see real deregulation for a long time," predicted MacMurray. "In countries like China, Indonesia and India, where there are large bureaucracies, it is very difficult to deregulate very quickly."
